title: Nimbus pilot QA & benchmark scoping
summary: Kickoff for a short pilot to validate quality and performance for Nimbus's document summarization and extraction feature. Discussed success criteria (accuracy, hallucination tolerance, latency), workload sizing (avg/peak QPS, throughput), benchmark plan (golden prompts, regression suites, hallucination checks), and a proposed 6-week timeline with deliverables and security checks.
topics: Success criteria: accuracy/f1, hallucination rate, format adherence
Workload sizing: daily volume, peak QPS, concurrency
Benchmark design: golden prompts, regression playlists, synthetic vs replay
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark template and golden prompt doc (Samir) - target 2026-11-20
Nimbus to provide 500 representative docs + 100 edge-case samples (Jordan) - target 2026-11-22
Set up test VPC and credentials for a private pilot (Tom) - target 2026-11-25
Ria to run initial synthetic load test and share baseline latency/cost estimate - target 2026-11-27
Schedule tech deep dive for hallucination detection rules with Compliance (Lena + Ria) - target 2026-11-30
action_items: Samir: Send pricing and pilot contract template (due: 2026-11-20)
Jordan: Export 500 sample documents and 100 edge cases, anonymized (due: 2026-11-22)
Tom: Provision a test VPC and service account, share connection details (due: 2026-11-25)
Ria: Draft initial golden-prompt set and regression playlist and run smoke tests (due: 2026-11-27)
Lena: Provide compliance checklist and any additional data residency requirements (due: 2026-11-24)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Ria Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Nimbus ML Eng), Priya Sharma (Product), Tom Ortega (Infra), Lena Voss (Compliance)

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — Samir here on the AE side, and Ria is our solutions engineer. Appreciate you taking the time, Jordan, Priya, Tom, Lena. We thought today we'd align on success criteria for the pilot, the workload shape, and then dig into the quality evaluation plan — golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination checks etc. Sound good?

[00:22] Jordan: Yep, good to go. We're excited to see how Redwood performs on our summarization/extraction flows. Main ask: keep hallucinations low and maintain a strict output JSON schema for downstream processing.

[00:38] Ria: Great — can you give us a quick read on traffic? avg requests per day, typical docs sizes, peak qps, concurrency? That drives batching and latency tradeoffs.

[00:52] Jordan: Sure. Avg about 50k requests a day right now, average doc ~800 tokens, normalized after OCR. Peak burst toward end of day hits up to 120 QPS, sustained peaks around 60 QPS for a few minutes. Concurrency to downstream is normally 10-15 workers.

[01:15] Priya: Also worth noting we have heavy enterprise SLAs for some customers — 95th percentile latency ideally <300ms but if we can be <200ms even better. Cost matters, but reliability and correctness are top.

[01:37] Tom: infra constraints — everything must go through our VPC. If Redwood can do private deployment or a VPC peering with strict egress rules, that's preferred. KMS for encryption, and audit logs.

[01:50] Samir: Understood — Redwood Private works with VPC peering and customer-managed KMS; we also have Hosted with token-level retention options if you want to start faster. For the success criteria: let's try to convert those into measurable thresholds. Proposing: accuracy/F1 on extraction fields >= 0.92 on golden set, hallucination rate <1% on sample, format compliance >= 99% for the JSON output, 95th latency <300ms for small prompts, and cost estimate within your target. Thoughts?

[02:22] Lena: From compliance perspective, hallucinations impacting PII redaction are the main risk. If hallucination leads to extraneous PHI, that could be a blocker. So we need explicit checks for hallucination where model invents entities not present in source. Also need retention policy — logs only stored with our consent.

[02:48] Ria: We'll bake in a hallucination detection test — two approaches: rule-based heuristics that check for entity presence versus model output, and a human-labeled regression set we run during the pilot. We can run both and report the overlap.

[03:08] Jordan: For golden prompts — what's your suggestion for how many and how to structure? We have several document types: invoices, contracts, support transcripts.

[03:22] Ria: Recommend starting with 40 golden prompts distributed across doc types: 15 invoice, 10 contracts, 10 transcripts, 5 edge cases. Each golden prompt will have the expected output JSON and a small rubric with critical fields, allowable synonyms, and strict format rules. These prompts will be used for nightly regression and for the initial scoring.

[03:46] Samir: Important: include negative prompts — cases where model should return an empty extraction or explicit "no entity" token. That catches hallucinations where the model invents fields.

[04:02] Priya: How do you suggest scoring? Single metric or composite? We want a simple pass/fail for business teams, but also granular breakdowns for model engineers.

[04:16] Ria: We usually report a composite score: weighted combination where critical fields (e.g., legal party names, amounts) are weighted higher. Provide per-field F1, overall schema compliance, hallucination count per 1k requests, and a composite score scaled 0-100. Also provide thresholds: composite >= 85 is green, 70-85 yellow, <70 red. We'll customize weights with you.

[04:46] Jordan: Sounds reasonable. For load testing — we want both replay of real traffic and synthetic stress tests to validate autoscaling. Can Redwood run a replay against a dedicated pool?

[04:58] Ria: Yes — we can take a replay of a sample subset (anonymized) and run it against Redwood Dedicated or Private. For the pilot we'll provision a small dedicated pool to match your peak QPS and run both steady-state and burst tests. We'll capture latency percentiles, token throughput, and cost per 1k tokens.

[05:19] Tom: A note on model variants — we need the ability to fallback to a smaller quantized model if larger models hit capacity. Does Redwood support automated fallback?

[05:29] Samir: Yep — we have model variant routing and automatic fallback policies. For the pilot we can simulate fallbacks and measure delta in quality & latency. We'll document the compatibility matrix — some LLMs degrade more gracefully than others.

[05:45] Lena: On the compliance side, can we have an audit log of every inference with request ID, model version, and response hash? We'll need that for post-mortem.

[05:56] Ria: Yes — audit logs with request/response hashes and model version metadata are included in our Private offering. We can filter retention settings and export logs to your SIEM.

[06:10] Jordan: Back to golden prompts and regression — how often do you recommend we run full regression during pilot? Nightly vs weekly?

[06:23] Ria: For the pilot, nightly smoke checks on the golden set and full regression weekly is a good balance. If you detect drift or after a model change we'll run the full suite on demand.

[06:37] Priya: And what about hallucination checks — automatic vs manual? We don't have bandwidth for full manual labeling.

[06:47] Ria: We'll run automated heuristics that flag potential hallucinations, then sample those for manual review. For examples where high severity is suspected (PII fabrication) we'll prioritize manual review. We can also set up active sampling — e.g., review 10 flagged items/day.

[07:05] Tom: For workload sizing — Jordan mentioned avg doc 800 tokens. For batching decisions we need expected token distribution. Can you share percentiles (p50/p90/p99)?

[07:17] Jordan: Sure, p50 ~620 tokens, p90 ~1200, p99 ~2200 (rare long contracts). We'll include a histogram in the data dump.

[07:29] Ria: Good. We'll recommend an inference config: dynamic batching with max batch size tuned to keep 95th latency < 300ms for p90 inputs; and an option to bypass batching for latency-sensitive small prompts. We'll provide a config file.

[07:47] Samir: Timeline — propose a 6-week pilot: week 0 (setup & provisioning), week 1-2 (golden prompt construction & golden-set labeling), week 3-4 (run benchmarks and load tests), week 5 (regression analysis and tuning), week 6 (final report + decision). We can compress if Nimbus needs faster results.

[08:09] Priya: That's tight but doable. We prefer a 4-week minimum to have enough regression runs, but let's keep 6 weeks as default.

[08:20] Ria: On instrumentation: we'd like to provision a route in your staging so we can emit per-request metadata (request_id, model_version, tokens_in/out, latency) to our observability pipeline. That data helps correlate quality issues with latency or token patterns.

[08:37] Jordan: We'll provide a staging route in the VPC. Tom will share credentials and the peering route.

[08:46] Tom: Yes, I'll get that done. We'll also set up a service account restricted to staging.

[08:52] Lena: A quick question on data retention — we need inference logs to be retained for 90 days and encrypted at rest with our KMS. Can Redwood accommodate?

[09:01] Samir: Yes, retention policy and customer-managed KMS for Private deployments — we can configure retention to 90 days and rotate keys per your policy. For hosted, we can do shorter retention unless you sign a private contract.

[09:15] Jordan: On success criteria reporting, we need a simple dashboard for product to sign off. Can Redwood produce a weekly report with pass/fail on the golden set plus the composite score and hallucination incidents?

[09:27] Ria: Absolutely, we'll provision a dashboard and weekly summary PDF. We'll also attach the raw regression results and per-field metrics.

[09:38] Priya: If we find the hallucination rate is too high, what remediation options do you recommend? Prompt engineering, model variant, post-processing rules?

[09:48] Ria: All three. We start with prompt/system message adjustments and golden-prompt constraints. If needed, apply post-processing validators (entity cross-checks against source), and if that doesn't suffice, evaluate a different model or fine-tune/adapter approach. We can prototype rule-based validators quickly.

[10:05] Samir: Let's capture a concrete example for the regression playlist: e.g., a contract where the model must extract party name, effective date, and termination clause. Scoring: party name exact or alias allowed, date parsed to ISO, termination clause boolean with evidence span. We'll add that to the template.

[10:29] Jordan: For scoring thresholds: party name exact match 1.0, alias 0.8; date parse tolerance within one day 0.9; clause detection F1 target 0.85. Composite computed by weighted average.

[10:45] Ria: Noted. We'll also include a hallucination penalty in the composite — each hallucinated critical field subtracts a fixed delta.

[11:00] Priya: About golden prompts — please keep them human readable and include an "expected output" and a short rationale for edge cases. Product will use that to sign off.

[11:12] Samir: We'll deliver a Google Doc with the golden prompts and expected outputs and a CSV export for machines. Samir to share link.

[11:22] Jordan: For regression data labeling — do you recommend Redwood label or Nimbus label? We have limited labeling capacity.

[11:31] Ria: We can do a hybrid: Redwood labels the golden set and initial regression samples; Nimbus reviews and signs off on critical cases. For larger sets, we can provide a labeling UI and suggest a small sample for human review. Labeling costs and SLAs can be included in the pilot SOW.

[11:50] Tom: On cost — would like a delta on cost per 1k tokens for each model variant and an estimate for your dedicated pool.

[11:59] Samir: We'll include a cost matrix. Ria will run an initial cost run and estimate expected monthly token spend under your traffic profile.

[12:10] Lena: One more compliance question — will Redwood support an on-site audit if needed? Some of our customers require that.

[12:18] Samir: We support audit-friendly artifacts and can coordinate with our security team on audit requests; on-site audits can be arranged for enterprise contracts under NDA — we'll flag that for the procurement thread.

[12:31] Priya: Great. Anything else we should capture?

[12:36] Jordan: I'd like to add a specific hallucination check: for named-entity outputs, cross-check against source text; flag any entity where no substring match exists unless it's in an allowed alias list.

[12:49] Ria: We'll include that in the regression validators as a required rule.

[12:56] Samir: Okay, let's recap action items and timeline briefly...

[13:02] Samir: Redwood: share benchmark template, golden prompt starter set, cost matrix, and pilot SOW by 2026-11-20. Nimbus: provide samples, provision staging VPC and creds, and review compliance checklist by noted dates. Ria will run smoke tests and baseline. We'll meet again after initial data handoff, tentatively 2026-11-29 for a tech deep dive.

[13:27] Jordan: Works for us.

[13:30] Tom: I'll start the VPC work tomorrow.

[13:33] Lena: I'll review and send any additional compliance items.

[13:36] Samir: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with links and the SOW. End of call.

Notes: Transcript contains occasional mis-hearings and abbreviated speaker tags; timestamps approximate.
